pos: n. (a figure in Daniel's visions for a late-arising power that persecutes the saints)
etymology: English little + horn, rendering Aramaic qeren ze'eyrah in Daniel 7:8 and Hebrew qeren achath tse'irah in Daniel 8:9. The horn is the standing biblical figure for kingly power, so a little horn is a power that begins small and grows.
biblical_def: The little horn is the figure Daniel twice receives for a kingly power that rises after others, begins small, and grows into a persecutor of the people of God. In the vision of the four beasts the fourth beast has ten horns, and Daniel says, “I considered the horns, and, behold, there came up among them another little horn, before whom there were three of the first horns plucked up by the roots: and, behold, in this horn were eyes like the eyes of man, and a mouth speaking great things.” The eyes mark intelligence and the mouth marks blasphemy. The interpreting angel is explicit about what this power does: it “shall speak great words against the most High, and shall wear out the saints of the most High, and think to change times and laws.” A second little horn appears in the vision of the ram and the he goat, coming “out of one of them” and waxing “exceeding great, toward the south, and toward the east, and toward the pleasant land.” The two are not the same power; the eighth-chapter horn arises out of the Grecian kingdom, and the seventh-chapter horn out of the fourth beast. What they share is the pattern: a power small at first, speaking against heaven, making war upon the saints, and holding them for an appointed and limited season. The appointed limit is the comfort of the passage — the horn makes war and prevails, but only “until a time and times and the dividing of time,” and then the judgment sits.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): Horn, a symbol of strength and of regal power; in prophetick language, a kingdom or dynasty. A little horn, a power small in its beginning which afterward grows great.
webster_full: Horn, in Scripture, a symbol of strength, and of regal or political power.
In prophetick language, a horn signifies a kingdom, a dynasty, or a ruler.
Ten horns, Daniel 7:7, the ten powers of the fourth beast.
A little horn, Daniel 7:8 and 8:9, a power small at its rise and afterward exceeding great.
To push with the horn, to war against; to break the horn, to destroy the power.
scriptures: Dan 7:8

I considered the horns, and, behold, there came up among them another little horn, before whom there were three of the first horns plucked up by the roots: and, behold, in this horn were eyes like the eyes of man, and a mouth speaking great things.
Dan 8:9
And out of one of them came forth a little horn, which waxed exceeding great, toward the south, and toward the east, and toward the pleasant land.
Dan 7:21
I beheld, and the same horn made war with the saints, and prevailed against them;
Dan 7:25

And he shall speak great words against the most High, and shall wear out the saints of the most High, and think to change times and laws: and they shall be given into his hand until a time and times and the dividing of time.
corruption_summary: The little horn is handed over to newspaper prophecy and read as a coded reference to whichever present ruler alarms the reader, while the text's own point — that persecution is permitted, measured, and ended by God — is lost.
corruption_paragraphs: The dominant modern treatment is prediction-chasing. Nineteenth-century dispensationalism, following Darby and popularised by the Scofield Reference Bible, detached the little horn from the flow of redemptive history and placed it in a future seven-year parenthesis, after which every generation of readers has been invited to identify the horn with a living politician. The method is self-refuting, since each identification is quietly dropped and replaced, and it trains Christians to read Daniel for the thrill of decoding rather than for the endurance the book was written to produce. The Reformers and the Puritans read the seventh-chapter horn as the papal power precisely because they read it historically rather than sensationally, and whatever a reader concludes about that identification, the method was the sounder one.

The second corruption runs the other way. Historical-critical scholarship dates Daniel to the second century before Christ and treats the little horn of chapter eight as a record of Antiochus Epiphanes written after the fact, which dissolves prophecy into pious fraud and denies the book its own claim to have been given to Daniel in the sixth century. The dictionary holds the sixth-century Daniel, and with it the plain sense of Daniel 2:45, that “the dream is certain, and the interpretation thereof sure.” Between sensationalism and unbelief the text itself is sober: a power will speak great words, wear out the saints, and be given a measured span, and then the Ancient of days will sit in judgment. That is written for the comfort of persecuted believers, not for the curiosity of comfortable ones.
roots_summary: Aramaic qeren, a horn, hence a king or kingdom; ze'eyrah, little, small; the figure of a power small at its rise and great in its blasphemy.
roots_lines: Aramaic qeren, a horn; in prophecy a king or a kingdom, Daniel 7:24.
Aramaic ze'eyrah, little, small, Daniel 7:8.
Hebrew qeren tse'irah, a little horn, Daniel 8:9.
The horn has eyes and a mouth, marking intelligence and blasphemy, Daniel 7:8.
Its span is limited to a time and times and the dividing of time, Daniel 7:25.

pos: n. phr. (the stone of Nebuchadnezzar's dream, figure of Christ's kingdom)
etymology: English rendering of Aramaic eben, a stone, with di la bidayin, “which not by hands,” in Daniel 2:34. The negative is the whole force of the phrase: the stone is quarried by no human agency.
biblical_def: In Nebuchadnezzar's dream a great image stands composed of gold, silver, brass, iron, and iron mixed with clay, and it is destroyed not by an army but by a stone. “Thou sawest till that a stone was cut out without hands, which smote the image upon his feet that were of iron and clay, and brake them to pieces.” Daniel's interpretation makes the stone a kingdom: “And in the days of these kings shall the God of heaven set up a kingdom, which shall never be destroyed.” The phrase without hands is the doctrinal centre. Every kingdom in the image was raised by human hands, by conquest and succession and policy, and every one of them is reduced together to “the chaff of the summer threshingfloors” which “the wind carried… away.” The stone is of another order altogether. It is cut out of the mountain by God, it grows until it “became a great mountain, and filled the whole earth,” and it does not share the earth with the kingdoms it struck. The dictionary takes the stone as Christ and His kingdom, which is the reading the New Testament itself presses when it sets Christ before us as the stone of stumbling and the head of the corner. The dream is given to a pagan king at the height of his power, and its message to him is that his gold head will become chaff and that the kingdom which lasts is one no hand of his can build or break.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): Stone, a hard concretion of earthy matter; figuratively, firmness and durableness. Cut out without hands, made without human agency, as the stone of Daniel 2:34, signifying a kingdom of divine and not human founding.
webster_full: Stone, a hard, solid concretion of earthy or mineral matter.
Figuratively, firmness, durableness, that which cannot be moved.
In Scripture, Christ is called a stone, a corner stone, a stone of stumbling.
Cut out without hands, Daniel 2:34, formed by no human agency.
The stone became a great mountain and filled the whole earth, Daniel 2:35.
scriptures: Dan 2:34
Thou sawest till that a stone was cut out without hands, which smote the image upon his feet that were of iron and clay, and brake them to pieces.
Dan 2:35

Then was the iron, the clay, the brass, the silver, and the gold, broken to pieces together, and became like the chaff of the summer threshingfloors; and the wind carried them away, that no place was found for them: and the stone that smote the image became a great mountain, and filled the whole earth.
Dan 2:44

And in the days of these kings shall the God of heaven set up a kingdom, which shall never be destroyed: and the kingdom shall not be left to other people, but it shall break in pieces and consume all these kingdoms, and it shall stand for ever.
Dan 2:45

Forasmuch as thou sawest that the stone was cut out of the mountain without hands, and that it brake in pieces the iron, the brass, the clay, the silver, and the gold; the great God hath made known to the king what shall come to pass hereafter: and the dream is certain, and the interpretation thereof sure.
corruption_summary: The stone is read as a symbol of human moral progress or of the church's cultural achievement, when its defining mark is precisely that no human hand quarried it.
corruption_paragraphs: The commonest misuse makes the stone a figure for gradual human improvement — the slow civilising of the nations, the advance of justice, the leaven of Christian values in culture. Every version of this reading contradicts the one thing the text insists upon. The stone is cut out without hands, and the kingdoms it destroys are precisely the ones hands built. A reading that turns the stone into the achievement of the church, or of the West, or of a political programme, has replaced the kingdom God sets up with a kingdom men set up and has thereby identified the stone with the image. Daniel 2:44 is explicit that it is “the God of heaven” who sets the kingdom up.

A second misuse is quieter and more respectable: the stone is granted its divine origin but its finality is removed, so that Christ's kingdom becomes one legitimate option among the world's kingdoms, holding a private sphere while the iron and clay keep the public one. Daniel will not allow the division. The stone smites the image, the whole of it goes to chaff together, and the stone fills the whole earth. The classical two-kingdoms doctrine distinguishes the spheres of church and magistrate without conceding that Christ's reign is partial; the radical two-kingdoms position, which severs the civil sphere from His lordship altogether, is the modern form of the error Daniel 2 forecloses. What is to be recovered here is simple confidence: the kingdom that is coming was not built by us, cannot be broken by them, and will not finally share the ground.
roots_summary: Aramaic eben, a stone; di la bidayin, which not by hands; the kingdom of God as divinely and not humanly founded.
roots_lines: Aramaic eben, a stone, Daniel 2:34.

pos: n. phr. (the clear expanse before the throne of God in the Revelation)
etymology: English rendering of Greek thalassa hyalinē, a glassy sea, from hyalos, glass or crystal. The figure recalls the molten sea of Solomon's temple and the pavement of sapphire under the God of Israel in Exodus 24:10.
biblical_def: John sees before the throne “a sea of glass like unto crystal,” and later “a sea of glass mingled with fire.” The sea in Scripture is ordinarily the restless and threatening element, the deep that must be rebuked, the place from which the beast rises. Before the throne it is a sea no longer in motion. It is solid, clear, and still, and the saints stand upon it. That is the whole doctrine of the figure: what is turbulent and hostile in this world is, in the presence of God, floored and transparent. The second vision adds fire to the crystal and sets upon it “them that had gotten the victory over the beast, and over his image, and over his mark, and over the number of his name,” holding “the harps of God.” The fire is the fire of judgment through which they passed, and the glass is the firmness on which they now stand to sing. The temple furniture lies behind the image — the laver of brass in which the priests washed stood between the altar and the holy place, and Solomon's molten sea served the same cleansing office — so that the sea of glass marks the court of a sanctuary where the washing is finished and nothing remains to be cleansed. There is no longer any water to be used, because there is no longer any defilement to remove.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): Glass, a hard, brittle, transparent substance. A sea of glass, Revelation 4:6, an expanse clear as crystal before the throne, the figure of a perfect transparency and stillness in the presence of God.
webster_full: Glass, a hard, brittle, transparent, factitious substance.
Used figuratively of perfect clearness and of that which hides nothing.
A sea of glass like unto crystal, Revelation 4:6, before the throne.
A sea of glass mingled with fire, Revelation 15:2, whereon the victors stand.
Compare the molten sea of the temple, 1 Kings 7:23, and the laver of brass.
scriptures: Rev 4:6
And before the throne there was a sea of glass like unto crystal: and in the midst of the throne, and round about the throne, were four beasts full of eyes before and behind.
Rev 15:2

And I saw as it were a sea of glass mingled with fire: and them that had gotten the victory over the beast, and over his image, and over his mark, and over the number of his name, stand on the sea of glass, having the harps of God.
And they saw the God of Israel: and there was under his feet as it were a paved work of a sapphire stone, and as it were the body of heaven in his clearness.
And the building of the wall of it was of jasper: and the city was pure gold, like unto clear glass.
corruption_summary: The sea of glass is treated as scenic decoration in an exotic vision rather than as the sanctuary figure it is — the chaos of the world made still and the cleansing finished.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. What it faces instead is neglect, and a particular kind of neglect: the Revelation's throne-room furniture is read as atmosphere. Commentators and readers alike move quickly past the sea of glass toward the parts of the book that can be turned into a timeline, and in doing so they lose the one detail the figure exists to carry. John is describing a sanctuary. The sea before the throne answers to the laver before the holy place, and the saints standing on it are standing where water used to be needed. That is a statement about the completeness of the cleansing accomplished by Christ, and it is of a piece with the later word that in the city there is no temple and no need of the sun.

The principle to recover is that the images of Revelation are drawn from the tabernacle and the temple, and are read rightly only by a reader who knows that furniture. The sea of glass is not a decorative flourish; it is the still, floored, transparent answer to Genesis 1:2 and to every sea in the Psalms that roars and will not be quiet. Mingled with fire, it says that the saints who stand there came through judgment and were not consumed. The right response to the figure is the response the text itself records — they stand, and they have the harps of God, and they sing the song of Moses and of the Lamb.
roots_summary: Greek thalassa, a sea; hyalinē, glassy, from hyalos, glass or crystal; a still and transparent expanse before the throne.
roots_lines: Greek thalassa, the sea, in Scripture often the restless and hostile deep.
Greek hyalos, glass, crystal; hyalinē, glassy, transparent.
Like unto crystal, Revelation 4:6, marking perfect clearness.
Mingled with fire, Revelation 15:2, the judgment the victors passed through.
Answers to the laver of brass and the molten sea of the temple.

pos: n. phr. (the final series of judgments in the Revelation, poured from seven vials)
etymology: English plague, from Latin plaga, a blow or stroke, rendering Greek plēgē, a stroke, wound, or calamity; with hepta, seven, and eschatos, last.
biblical_def: John writes, “And I saw another sign in heaven, great and marvellous, seven angels having the seven last plagues; for in them is filled up the wrath of God.” The word last is the governing word of the phrase, and the clause that follows explains it: in these the wrath of God is filled up. These are not simply the latest of a series but the completion of it, the point at which the cup is full and nothing further is added. The Greek plēgē is a stroke or a blow, and the series deliberately recalls the plagues of Egypt — waters turned to blood, sores, darkness, frogs, hail — so that the reader is meant to see the God of the Exodus acting again, and on the same terms. The seven angels come out of the temple “clothed in pure and white linen, and having their breasts girded with golden girdles,” which is priestly dress; the judgments proceed from the sanctuary and not from caprice. Then “the temple was filled with smoke from the glory of God, and from his power; and no man was able to enter into the temple, till the seven plagues of the seven angels were fulfilled” — a sober detail, for it marks a season in which intercession is no longer being made. The last appearance of the phrase turns the whole scene round: one of these same seven angels carries John to see “the bride, the Lamb's wife.”
webster_summary: Webster (1828): Plague, a stroke, an affliction, a calamity sent as a divine judgment. The seven last plagues, Revelation 15:1, in which the wrath of God is filled up.
webster_full: Plague, any thing troublesome or vexatious; particularly, a pestilential disease.
From Latin plaga, a stroke or blow; Greek plēgē, a stroke, wound, calamity.
In Scripture, a divine judgment sent upon men, as the plagues of Egypt.
The seven last plagues, Revelation 15:1, poured out of seven vials.
Called last because in them is filled up the wrath of God.
scriptures: Rev 15:1
And I saw another sign in heaven, great and marvellous, seven angels having the seven last plagues; for in them is filled up the wrath of God.
Rev 15:6
And the seven angels came out of the temple, having the seven plagues, clothed in pure and white linen, and having their breasts girded with golden girdles.
Rev 15:8
And the temple was filled with smoke from the glory of God, and from his power; and no man was able to enter into the temple, till the seven plagues of the seven angels were fulfilled.
Rev 21:9
And there came unto me one of the seven angels which had the seven vials full of the seven last plagues, and talked with me, saying, Come hither, I will shew thee the bride, the Lamb's wife.
corruption_summary: The series is mined for a calendar of end-time disasters, while the clause that defines it — that in these the wrath of God is filled up — and the doctrine of divine wrath itself are passed over.
corruption_paragraphs: The popular use is a timeline. The vials are matched to wars, epidemics, ecological disasters, and political events, and the exercise is repeated in every generation with the same confidence and the same silent abandonment of the previous attempt. This is the method of the prophecy-chart industry that grew out of nineteenth-century dispensationalism, and it fails on its own terms, but it also fails the text. Revelation 15:1 supplies the definition of last in the same sentence — “for in them is filled up the wrath of God” — and that is a statement about completion and not about a date. A reader who finishes the chapter knowing when and not knowing what has learnt nothing the chapter teaches.

The deeper corruption is the quiet removal of wrath from the character of God. Across much modern preaching divine wrath is reinterpreted as the impersonal operation of consequences, or as a primitive conception the New Testament outgrew, or as inconsistent with love; the vials then become metaphors for the world's self-inflicted damage. Scripture does not allow the softening. The wrath here is God's own, it is measured, it is filled up to a completion He appoints, and it proceeds from His temple carried by priests. The Reformed doctrine holds wrath and love together in the same God without embarrassment, which is exactly why the cross stands at the centre: the wrath is real, and it was borne. The principle to recover is that the same angel who pours out a vial is the angel who shows John the bride, and both offices belong to one God.

pos: n. phr. (the number six hundred threescore and six, Revelation 13:18)
etymology: English number, from Latin numerus, rendering Greek arithmos; with thērion, a wild beast. The number is given in the Authorized Version in words, “Six hundred threescore and six.”
biblical_def: At the close of the thirteenth chapter of the Revelation John writes, “Here is wisdom. Let him that hath understanding count the number of the beast: for it is the number of a man; and his number is Six hundred threescore and six.” The number is distinguished in the text from the mark and from the name: no man might buy or sell “save he that had the mark, or the name of the beast, or the number of his name.” Three things are therefore in view, and the number is the third. Two statements in the verse govern every honest reading of it. First, it is offered to understanding and not to curiosity — “Here is wisdom” is an invitation to the wise, and the wisdom in question throughout the Revelation is the wisdom that endures and keeps the commandments of God. Second, “it is the number of a man,” which sets the beast, for all its heads and horns and blasphemy, on the creaturely side of the line. The number is a man's number. Against the sevens that fill the book — seven churches, seven seals, seven spirits — a number that falls short of seven three times over is a figure of the beast's inability ever to arrive. Those who overcome are later described as having gotten the victory “over the number of his name,” which is the pastoral end of the whole matter.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): Number, a collection of units; also a figure or numeral. The number of the beast, Revelation 13:18, six hundred sixty-six, declared to be the number of a man.
webster_full: Number, a collection or assemblage of units; the designation of quantity.
Also a numeral figure or character used to express quantity.
The number of the beast, Revelation 13:18, given as Six hundred threescore and six.
Declared in the same verse to be the number of a man.
Distinguished from the mark and from the name of the beast, Revelation 13:17.
scriptures: Here is wisdom. Let him that hath understanding count the number of the beast: for it is the number of a man; and his number is Six hundred threescore and six.
And that no man might buy or sell, save he that had the mark, or the name of the beast, or the number of his name.
Rev 15:2

And I saw as it were a sea of glass mingled with fire: and them that had gotten the victory over the beast, and over his image, and over his mark, and over the number of his name, stand on the sea of glass, having the harps of God.
Here is the patience of the saints: here are they that keep the commandments of God, and the faith of Jesus.
corruption_summary: The number is treated as a cipher to be cracked and then as an occult brand to be feared, when the verse itself calls for wisdom and endurance and says the number belongs to a man.
corruption_paragraphs: The number has been made the property of prophecy speculation, and the harvest is a long record of confident calculations quietly abandoned. Gematria has been run on emperors, popes, reformers, chancellors, presidents, and corporations; dispensational popularisers have attached it to bar codes, implanted chips, identity numbers, and payment systems in turn. The method mistakes the verse's own instruction. “Here is wisdom” is not a promise that the arithmetically clever will identify a man before he arrives; it is the Revelation's recurring summons to the understanding that perseveres, the same summons as “Here is the patience of the saints.” A reading that produces excitement and a datable prediction has produced the opposite of what the verse asks for.

The second corruption is the treatment of the number as a thing with power in itself, an occult sign whose accidental appearance on a receipt or an address is a spiritual threat. This is superstition, and it concedes to the beast exactly the standing the text denies him: “it is the number of a man.” Scripture nowhere teaches that a numeral can defile, and the believer's security does not depend on avoiding a sequence of digits. What Revelation 15:2 promises is that the saints get the victory over the number of his name, and what Revelation 14:12 describes is how — they keep the commandments of God and the faith of Jesus. The principle to recover is that the number is a measure of the beast's limit, not of his reach.
roots_summary: Greek arithmos, a number; thērion, a wild beast; the number of a man, falling thrice short of seven, the figure of a power that never arrives.

pos: n. phr. (the fourth horse of the seals, whose rider is Death)
etymology: English pale, from Latin pallidus, rendering Greek chlōros, pale green, the colour of withered grass or of a corpse. The same Greek word is rendered “green” of grass elsewhere in the Revelation.
biblical_def: The fourth seal brings the last of the four horses: “And I looked, and behold a pale horse: and his name that sat on him was Death, and Hell followed with him. And power was given unto them over the fourth part of the earth, to kill with sword, and with hunger, and with death, and with the beasts of the earth.” Of the four riders this is the only one named, and he is named twice over, for Death rides and Hell comes behind. The colour is not whiteness but the sick green-grey of a corpse; the Greek word is the one used of green grass, and applied to a horse it gives the pallor of a thing with the life gone out of it. The rider's commission is bounded, as every commission in the seals is bounded: power over “the fourth part of the earth,” and four named instruments — sword, hunger, death, and the beasts of the earth — which are the four judgments God names together in Ezekiel 14:21. Two things are therefore true at once and must be held together. Death is a real rider with real authority, going out over the earth; and the authority is given, measured, and limited by the One who opened the seal. The Lamb opens it. That is the single fact that keeps the vision from being despair, and it is why the chapter can be read by Christians facing plague and war without being crushed by it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): Pale, white in countenance; wanting colour; deprived of the natural and lively hue. A pale horse, Revelation 6:8, whose rider is Death.
webster_full: Pale, white or whitish in countenance; wanting colour or lustre.
Deprived of the natural and lively hue, as the pallor of the dead.
Greek chlōros, pale green, elsewhere rendered green of grass, Revelation 8:7.
A pale horse, Revelation 6:8, the fourth of the horses of the seals.
His rider alone of the four is named: his name that sat on him was Death.
scriptures: Rev 6:8

And I looked, and behold a pale horse: and his name that sat on him was Death, and Hell followed with him. And power was given unto them over the fourth part of the earth, to kill with sword, and with hunger, and with death, and with the beasts of the earth.
Rev 6:7
And when he had opened the fourth seal, I heard the voice of the fourth beast say, Come and see.
For thus saith the Lord GOD; How much more when I send my four sore judgments upon Jerusalem, the sword, and the famine, and the noisome beast, and the pestilence, to cut off from it man and beast?
Rev 1:18
I am he that liveth, and was dead; and, behold, I am alive for evermore, Amen; and have the keys of hell and of death.
corruption_summary: The pale horse is absorbed into general apocalyptic dread, so that Death appears sovereign and the detail that his power was given, and given over a fourth part only, is dropped.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The pale horse is instead flattened by use. It has become shorthand in popular speech for catastrophe without limit, and the borrowing is understandable, but it keeps exactly the terror of the image and discards its governing clauses. The text does not present Death as an autonomous force loose in the world. It says “power was given unto them,” and it fixes the scope at “the fourth part of the earth.” The seal is opened by the Lamb, which means the rider goes out at the command of the One who was dead and is alive and has the keys of hell and of death.

The principle to recover is the Reformed doctrine of providence applied where it is hardest to apply it. Sword, famine, pestilence, and wild beasts are the four judgments of Ezekiel 14:21, and Scripture does not pretend they are not dreadful or that the godly are exempt from them. It insists instead that they are instruments and not sovereigns, measured out and called back. A Christian reading the fourth seal in a time of war or epidemic is meant to see both things plainly: that the pale horse is really riding, and that the hand on the seal is the Lamb's. Nothing in the vision invites either denial or panic.

roots_lines: Greek hippos, a horse; the fourth of the horses of the seals.

pos: n. phr. (the third horse of the seals, and the horses of Zechariah's chariots)
etymology: English black, Old English blaec, rendering Greek melas in Revelation 6:5 and Hebrew shachor in Zechariah 6:2. The colour carries famine and mourning in Hebrew usage.
biblical_def: The Authorized Version uses the phrase in two prophets. In the Revelation the third seal brings it: “And when he had opened the third seal, I heard the third beast say, Come and see. And I beheld, and lo a black horse; and he that sat on him had a pair of balances in his hand.” The balances are scales, and the voice that follows prices wheat and barley at a day's wage for a day's bread while charging the rider to spare the oil and the wine. This is not famine as total crop failure but famine as ruinous scarcity, where food is available and unaffordable and the luxuries of the rich are untouched. It is a judgment that falls hardest on the poor, and the detail about the oil and the wine is a moral detail, not a botanical one. In Zechariah the black horses are among the teams of the four chariots that come from between two mountains of brass: “In the first chariot were red horses; and in the second chariot black horses.” These are the horses of God's patrols, and the black team goes out with a commission — “The black horses which are therein go forth into the north country” — the north being the quarter from which Israel's conquerors had come. In both prophets the colour is bound to want and to mourning, and in both the horse is under orders.

corruption_summary: The third seal is read as undifferentiated disaster, when the balances and the sparing of the oil and the wine make it a judgment specifically upon an economy that prices bread beyond the poor.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The failure here is a failure of attention to detail that Scripture has taken trouble to supply. The third seal is routinely summarised as “famine” and left there, which loses the balances. A pair of scales in a rider's hand is an instrument of commerce, and the voice that follows does not announce that there is no food; it announces a price. A measure of wheat for a penny, with a penny the day's wage of Matthew 20:2, is a day's labour for a day's bread and nothing over. The oil and the wine — the goods of the comfortable — are expressly spared. Scripture is describing a scarcity that sorts men by what they can pay.

The principle to recover is that God's judgments are discriminating and that Scripture's concern for just weights is of a piece with this vision. The law repeatedly forbids a false balance and the Proverbs call it an abomination; here a balance appears in the hand of a judgment-rider, and the bread of the poor is weighed out. Zechariah's black team, sent into the north country, makes the same point from the other side: these horses are patrols under orders, not accidents. The reader is meant to see both that such scarcity is a real visitation and that the hand that opened the seal is the Lamb's.

pos: n. phr. (the horse of Zechariah's first vision and of his first chariot)
etymology: English red, Old English read, rendering Hebrew adom, red, the colour of blood and the root behind Edom and Adam. The Authorized Version's phrase “red horse” belongs to Zechariah.
biblical_def: The exact phrase red horse is Zechariah's, and precision here matters, because the second seal of the Revelation is commonly quoted in these words and the Authorized Version does not use them there; Revelation 6:4 reads, “there went out another horse that was red.” Zechariah opens his night visions with one: “I saw by night, and behold a man riding upon a red horse, and he stood among the myrtle trees that were in the bottom; and behind him were there red horses, speckled, and white.” These are the LORD's patrols, sent “to walk to and fro through the earth,” and they return with a report — the earth sits still and at rest — which draws from the angel of the LORD the question how long Jerusalem will go uncomforted. The red horse appears again among the four chariots: “In the first chariot were red horses.” The colour is the colour of blood, and the Hebrew adom stands behind both Edom and Adam, the red man from the red earth. Taken together the visions teach that the earth's quiet is not God's indifference. The horses are out, the reports are coming in, and the question of Zechariah 1:12 — how long? — is answered in the next verse with good words and comfortable words.

corruption_summary: The red horse is routinely quoted from Revelation in words the Authorized Version does not use there, and Zechariah's visions of God's patrols are passed over as obscure.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. It faces a habit of inexactitude. “The red horse of the apocalypse” is so established a phrase that readers assume they are quoting Revelation 6:4, where the Authorized Version in fact reads “another horse that was red.” The phrase red horse is Zechariah's. Nothing doctrinal collapses on the point, but a dictionary that honours the Authorized Version ought to say which prophet said what, and the misattribution has a cost: it keeps attention on the seals and away from Zechariah's night visions, which are among the most pastorally direct passages in the prophets.

The principle to recover is the one Zechariah 1 exists to supply. The horses go out and come back to report, and the report is that the earth is at rest — which is precisely the complaint, since Jerusalem lies waste while the nations are comfortable. The angel asks how long, and the LORD answers with good and comfortable words and with the promise that His house shall be built. That is a message for believers who look at a settled and prosperous world that has no room for the worship of God and wonder whether anything is being noticed. Zechariah's answer is that the patrols are out and the reports are in.

pos: n. phr. (the resurrection of Revelation 20:5-6, on which the second death has no power)
etymology: English first + resurrection, from Latin resurgere, to rise again, rendering Greek anastasis hē prōtē, the first rising.
biblical_def: The phrase occurs twice, in a single passage. “But the rest of the dead lived not again until the thousand years were finished. This is the first resurrection. Blessed and holy is he that hath part in the first resurrection: on such the second death hath no power, but they shall be priests of God and of Christ, and shall reign with him a thousand years.” Three things the text states plainly, and they are the substance of the doctrine whatever a reader concludes about the millennial question. It is called first, which implies a second and sets this rising in an order. Those who share in it are pronounced “blessed and holy,” so that participation is not a neutral fact but a benediction. And its benefit is stated negatively and absolutely: “on such the second death hath no power.” The dictionary leaves the millennial position open within Reformed orthodoxy. Amillennial readers have taken the first resurrection as the believer's regeneration or his entrance upon the intermediate state, reigning with Christ in heaven during the present age; postmillennial and historic premillennial readers have taken it as a bodily rising. What is not open is the dispensational scheme, a nineteenth-century novelty appearing in no Reformation confession, which multiplies resurrections and judgments to fit a system. On any confessional reading the pastoral force is the same: those who have part in the first resurrection are beyond the reach of the second death.

corruption_summary: The passage is made the property of a millennial system, so that two verses about a benediction and a safety are read chiefly as evidence in a timetable dispute.
corruption_paragraphs: The first corruption is the dispensational one. Darby's system, carried into English-speaking Christianity by the Scofield Reference Bible and the popular prophecy writing that followed it, divides the resurrection into a series of stages fitted to a rapture, a tribulation, and a literal earthly millennium with a rebuilt temple and a renewed sacrificial system. No Reformation confession contains any of it. The cost is not merely schematic: a sacrificial system restored after Calvary contradicts the book of Hebrews, and a church set aside as a parenthesis in a programme for Israel divides the one people of God that Ephesians 2 says Christ made one. The dictionary holds the millennial question open among amillennialism, postmillennialism, and historic premillennialism, and holds the dispensational scheme outside the confessional line.

The second corruption is liberal and comes from the other direction: the resurrection language of the Revelation is treated as symbol only, a way of speaking about the triumph of ideals or the persistence of a community's hope, with no bodily rising of the dead at the end. That is not a reading of the text but a replacement of it, and it collides with the whole New Testament witness and with the Apostles' Creed. The principle to recover is the one both errors obscure. Revelation 20:6 is not primarily a datum for a chart; it is a beatitude. It says that the man who has part in this rising is blessed and holy and that the second death cannot touch him, and that is addressed to believers who were being killed for the witness of Jesus.

pos: n. phr. (Jude's figure for false teachers who keep no fixed course)
etymology: English wandering + stars, rendering Greek asteres planētai, from planētēs, a wanderer — the word behind English planet, and cognate with planē, error or deceit.
biblical_def: Jude piles up five figures for the false teachers who had crept in among the churches, and the last is this: “Raging waves of the sea, foaming out their own shame; wandering stars, to whom is reserved the blackness of darkness for ever.” The Greek is asteres planētai, and the noun is the one from which English takes planet — the wanderers, the lights that do not keep the fixed station of the constellations. The figure is drawn from navigation. A mariner sets his course by stars that hold their place; a star that wanders is not merely unusual, it is useless and worse than useless, because a man who steers by it is lost. That is Jude's charge against the teachers. They have light, or the appearance of it; they are conspicuous; and they cannot be steered by. The preceding figures run in the same direction — clouds that carry no water, trees that bear no fruit, waves that produce nothing but foam — and all four describe things that promise what they do not deliver. The sentence pronounced is darkness: “to whom is reserved the blackness of darkness for ever.” A light that will not hold its place ends in the dark, and the word reserved says the end is already appointed.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): Wandering, roving; unsettled; not keeping a fixed course. Wandering stars, Jude 13, the planets, which keep no fixed station; figuratively, teachers who hold no settled doctrine.
webster_full: Wandering, roving, rambling, unsettled, having no fixed course.
Greek planētēs, a wanderer, whence the English planet.
Cognate with planē, a wandering, hence error, deceit, delusion.

To whom is reserved the blackness of darkness for ever, Jude 13.

corruption_summary: Doctrinal restlessness is now praised as humility and growth, so that the very quality Jude names as damning — keeping no fixed station — is presented as the mark of an honest teacher.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern inversion is almost exact. To hold a settled confession is called rigidity; to abandon one position after another is called a journey, an evolving faith, a willingness to sit with the questions. Whole ministries are built on the public narration of doctrinal migration, and the migration itself is offered as the credential. Jude's metaphor answers this directly, because it is a metaphor about usefulness. The question is not whether a teacher has light but whether anyone can set a course by him. The deconstruction genre, in which a teacher dismantles the faith he once professed while retaining his platform and his audience, is the wandering star with a following, and the followers are the ones at sea.

Jude's own prescription stands against it in the same letter: contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints, building up yourselves on your most holy faith, keep yourselves in the love of God. The word once in verse three is the hinge; a faith once delivered is a fixed star and not a wandering one. None of this commends mere stubbornness or the refusal to be corrected by Scripture, which is a different fault with a different cure. The principle to recover is that teachers are to be judged by whether they hold the deposit, that constancy in doctrine is a pastoral mercy to the people who must navigate by it, and that Scripture reserves for the man who will not keep his station the blackness of darkness for ever.
